10.15.4.en: Many rich people lose their inner peace and live in terror for fear of losing their possessions through theft, so they feel their need of a fortified and safe city in which to put their treasures. Likewise many poor people are crushed by murmuring and discontent.

10.15.5.en: But from the spiritual side, the wealth of the rich man is his inner city, when his heart becomes the new Jerusalem from above, the icon of heaven, which no sin can slip into and no enemy can assault, so that the person lives rich with the heavens of God revealed within him. The poor man is the one whose eyes do not look to the inner wealth, and so he loses the One in whom we have a treasure.

10.15.6.en: * Wealth in itself is not an evil thing. "The ransom of a man's life are his riches" (Prov 13:3), for whoever gives to the poor redeems himself; therefore even in wealth there is room for virtue. You are like helmsmen on a great sea: if a man steers his course well he crosses the sea quickly and reaches the harbor, but the one who does not know how to manage his possessions well sinks in his cargo. So it is written: "The rich man's wealth is his strong city" (Prov 10:15).

10.15.7.en: St. Ambrose * To enjoy anything means to cling to it firmly for the sake of the thing itself. But to use something is to employ what we receive in order to obtain what we need, provided that it is fitting for us to need it.

10.15.8.en: * Do not think that silver or gold should be blamed because of the greedy, nor food and wine because of gluttons and drunkards, nor female beauty because of adulterers and fornicators. So it is in all other matters, especially when you see a physician using fire in a good way while a murderer uses bread containing poison to carry out his crime.

10.15.9.en: * When Job lost all his wealth and reached extreme poverty, he kept his soul undisturbed, fixed on God, to show that earthly things had no value in his eyes, but that he was greater than they, and God greater than he. If the men of our day had the same mind, we would not have been so persistently forbidden in the New Testament to possess these things in order to reach perfection. For our possessing such things without being attached to them is something more worthy of praise than not possessing them at all.

10.16.0.en: "The labour of the righteous tendeth to life:

10.16.1.en: the fruit of the wicked to sin" [16]

10.16.2.en: Perhaps the righteous man has nothing but the toil of his hands; he works in order to eat and live, and finds life and sweetness in his work. But the wicked man spends what he earns on sin, whether by his extravagance or by his stinginess. He squanders every blessing, and lives like one who is dead.

10.16.3.en: Some think that the righteous man puts his hand to honorable, lawful work that gives life its taste, offering what is for the building up of the community. But the wicked man puts his hand to improper works because they are more profitable, so he offers to others what is for their destruction, and his sins multiply into sins, and he continues in this without ceasing until he destroys himself and others.

10.16.4.en: * For we remember that we must be thankful to the Lord our God and Creator. We reject no fruit of His works; we use them in moderation and not in sinful excess. For this reason we do not fail to frequent the forums, the markets, the baths, the shops, the workshops, the inns, and all your business, and to keep all our other relations, so as to express our life with you in this world. With you we sail the sea, we enlist in military service, we till the soil and trade, and we sell openly the products of our commerce and our manufacture that you use.

10.16.5.en: Tertullian Origen says that no one is idle in the house of the wise man.

10.17.0.en: "He is in the way of life that keepeth instruction (discipline): but he that refuseth reproof erreth" [17]

10.17.1.en: A person lives as one on a journey toward heaven; the believer, keeping discipline, accepts counsel and so does not turn aside from the way of life. But the wicked man rejects counsel and does not accept discipline, so he goes astray and remains in his error.

10.17.2.en: * Just as the refiner of gold throws the piece of gold into the furnace so that it endures the fire for a time until he sees that it has been purified, so God permits the testing of human souls by tribulations until they are purified and obtain great benefit...

10.17.3.en: Let us not be troubled or despair when trials come upon us. For just as the refiner of gold knows the time the gold should be left in the furnace, and takes it out at the appointed time and does not leave it any longer in the fire lest it be spoiled and burned, how much more does God know this. When He sees that we have been greatly purified, He frees us from our trials, lest we be cast down and cast out because of the increase of our evils.

10.17.4.en: When something comes upon us that we did not expect, let us not murmur or lose heart, but receive it from God, who knows these things exactly, so that He tests our hearts by fire as He pleases, doing this for the benefit of those who are tried. Therefore the wise man commands us to submit to God in all things, for He knows perfectly when to bring us out of the furnace of evil (Wisdom of Jesus 1:1-2).

10.17.5.en: It is fitting for us to submit to Him always, and to thank Him continually, bearing everything with contentment, whether He grants us blessings or gives us disciplines. For the latter are a kind of blessing.

10.17.6.en: For the physician is a physician not only when he allows us to bathe (in the baths)... or to go to pleasant gardens, but also when he uses the scalpel and the knife!

10.17.7.en: And the father is a father not only when he caresses his son, but also when he disciplines and punishes him...!

10.17.8.en: And since we know that God is more tender than all physicians, it is not for us to inquire into His dealings, nor to demand an account of them from Him, but He does what seems good in His sight. So let us not distinguish whether He frees us from trial or disciplines us, for in both ways He wishes to restore us to health and make us partners with Him, and He knows our different needs, and what suits each one of us, and how and in what way we must be saved...

10.17.9.en: Let us follow Him wherever He commands us, and not think much about whether He commands us to walk an easy, smooth way or a hard, rough way.

10.18.0.en: 18 He that hideth hatred with lying lips, and he that uttereth a slander, is a fool. 19 In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise. 20 The tongue of the just is as choice silver: the heart of the wicked is little worth. 21 The lips of the righteous feed (guide) many: but fools die for want of wisdom.

10.18.1.en: "He that hideth hatred with lying lips, and he that uttereth a slander, is a fool" [18]

10.18.2.en: The Book of Proverbs is concerned to speak of the sanctification of the mouth and the tongue, comparing the lips of the righteous with the lips of the fool. The first utters holy words, or yields his lips to the Lord Christ who dwells in him, who sanctifies them and uses them for the building up of the speaker's soul and the souls of the hearers. The second expresses what is in his depths of dryness and emptiness, even death; so his words come forth deadly to his own soul and to his hearers.

10.18.3.en: And in the New Testament St. James gave us his epistle, which some call "the Book of Proverbs of the New Testament," speaking of the danger of the tongue, making clear the following:

10.18.4.en: Let us be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19).

10.18.5.en: Whoever does not bridle his tongue is not religious (Jas 1:26).

10.18.6.en: A man is not counted a true believer unless his works match his words (Jas 2:14-24).

10.18.7.en: The tongue does great things despite its small size (Jas 3:5).

10.18.8.en: "The tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity" (Jas 3:6); "an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (Jas 3:8); "a fountain sending forth either blessing or cursing" (Jas 3:10), a tree bearing a certain fruit (Jas 3:12).

10.18.9.en: It is fitting that we not use it to swear by (Jas 5:12), and that we always be truthful in what we promise.

10.18.10.en: This book is concerned with the speech of man in daily life, for it reveals what is in the depths. Speech must be truthful and not false [18], it has its limits [20], so that it becomes precious [20] and satisfying [21].

10.18.11.en: In this proverb a contrast is presented between the one who hides his hatred by hypocrisy, offering honeyed false words, and the one who declares the hatred in his heart and slanders his brothers. The first is a hypocrite and the second is ignorant and foolish, and it is not fitting for us to choose between this one and that, for both are wicked. The right choice is not to bear hatred at all, neither in our hidden hearts nor in our pure words.

10.18.12.en: Whoever thinks he can hide his hatred from God, as though God did not perceive what is in his heart or his thought, speaks lies with his lips in a spirit of pride.

10.19.0.en: "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" [19]

10.19.1.en: "Who will set a watch before my mouth, and a seal of wisdom upon my lips, that I fall not suddenly by them, and that my tongue destroy me not?" (Sir 22:33).

10.19.2.en: The more we speak, the greater the likelihood of falling into error, and we are drawn into the desire to speak without ceasing. By this we fall into exaggeration in speech, which drives us unconsciously to lying. This habit also leads us to fall into anger and to rush into unrestrained passions, and we are often compelled to apologize. This is the way of ignorance or folly.

10.19.3.en: Whoever speaks much loses the way of wisdom, but whoever examines every word before he utters it is counted wise, and is able to offer good counsel.

10.19.4.en: It is fitting for the believer to utter only edifying words, so that he does not give account for every idle word.

10.19.5.en: * Keep the doors closed, and then evil thoughts will quickly submit to you.

10.19.6.en: * "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin." If you have a truly useful word, open your lips. But if there is no need to speak, be silent, for this is better!

10.19.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * The virtue of silence, especially in church, is very great. Do not let any divine utterance escape you, but listen to it and control your voice, and do not utter with your lips a word that you will later wish to take back. Do not be rash in speech, for truly in a multitude of words there is a multitude of sin.

10.19.8.en: * Set a door to your mouth, to be closed when that is necessary. Close it tightly so that no one can make your voice rise in anger, or make you answer ugly words with the like. You have read and heard "Be ye angry, and sin not"; therefore, although we become angry because of our nature and not by our will, our mouths must not utter a single evil word, for fear of falling into sin.

10.19.9.en: Rather our words must be humble and gentle, and so we subject our tongues to our minds.

10.19.10.en: Control your tongue by bridling it firmly. Govern it and set it straight with moderation. Weigh the words it utters in the scales of justice, so that if your meanings are serious, your speech will have meaning, and your words will have weight.

10.19.11.en: Those who obey this become longsuffering, kind, and meek, by controlling their mouths, governing their tongues, thinking before speaking, and weighing their words.

10.19.12.en: We must behave thus, lest our words, which ought to reflect the beauty of our inner life, show instead evil character.

10.19.13.en: * When a multitude of words comes, sin finds an entrance, for in this multitude of words that we speak, it is not possible to keep to the limits even in a small degree. And because of lack of prudence, you fall into error. Truly, to express our thoughts without weighing our words as is fitting is in itself a grievous sin.

10.19.14.en: St. Ambrose Origen sees that Solomon himself did not sin when he spoke many words in dealing with the subjects that appear in the books mentioned in Holy Scripture (Eccl 12:12). Nor did Paul sin when he prolonged his speech until midnight (Acts 20:7-10). For they and others spoke the word of God, who is the one Word who was in the beginning with God (Jn 1:1), the one Word who bears many diverse thoughts that reveal aspects of the one Word. But whoever speaks of matters other than the word of God sins by prolonging his speech. He says: [The saints are not talkative or garrulous, for they hold to the aim that is in harmony with the one Word.]

10.19.15.en: * Much speaking is a sign of lack of discipline.

10.19.16.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * And as the lazy mind falls step by step through not being on guard against idle talk, then it descends and utters harmful speech. We are content first to speak about the affairs of others, then the tongue gnaws away, slandering their lives, and finally we incline to open abuse. Thus, when we sow provocation, quarrels begin and fires flare up at the center of anger, and then the peace of the heart is extinguished. Therefore Solomon says well: "The beginning of strife is the letting out of water" (Prov 17:14); the letting out of water is nothing but the letting loose of the tongue in chatter. On the other hand the wise man says: "The words of a man's mouth are deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook" (Prov 18:4). Thus when we let out water, we become a fountain of strife and quarrels. And those who do not control their tongues break harmony. Therefore we read what is written: "As an archer who wounds all, so is he who hires a fool or hires deceivers" (Prov 26:10). Moreover, those who are addicted to much speaking depart altogether from the straight way of righteousness. Therefore the prophet testifies, saying: "A man of tongue shall not be established in the earth" (Ps 140:11). And Solomon also says: "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Prov 10:19). And therefore Isaiah says: "And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever" (Isa 32:17). This indicates that where there is no restraint of speech, the righteousness of the soul grows cold. Therefore James says: "If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain" (Jas 1:26). Likewise he also says: "Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19). And when he describes the power of the tongue he adds, saying: "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (Jas 3:8). For this reason the Truth Himself warns us, saying: "Every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment" (Mt 12:36). What is meant here is every idle word that is unjustified and unnecessary and aims at no benefit for godliness. Therefore, if we shall give account for every idle word, we ought to consider the punishment laid up for chatter that is harmful and carries all iniquity.

10.19.18.en: * Guard your tongues. That is, do not speak evil of your brothers. For whoever speaks evil of his brother angers God who dwells in him. What each one does to his fellow, he does to God.

10.19.19.en: St. Macarius the Great * If you cannot stop the mouth of one who speaks evil of a person, then at least keep your mouth from sharing in this matter.

10.19.20.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian * It is said of St. Augustine that he composed two lines of verse, which he wrote and hung in the dining room to put an end to the plague of slander. Their translation:

10.19.21.en: O you who slander the honor of another / and rob the standing of his monastery, / leave this place, flee, / for you shall not share in its good. It happened that some bishops, his friends, sat with him at the table. They began to backbite certain people and to slander them before him. The saint immediately advised them, saying to them: Either you erase these two lines or I will rise from the table.

10.19.22.en: * If you hear someone slandering another, flee from him as you would flee from a poisonous snake, until he is ashamed and learns not to speak so again.

10.20.0.en: St. Jerome "The tongue of the just is as choice silver: the heart of the wicked is little worth" [20]

10.20.1.en: What a person utters often reveals his character and declares what is in his heart. The man who has experienced the heavenly pledge brings forth words that are as though heavenly, and the one who values his precious life brings forth words like silver.

10.20.2.en: The tongue of the righteous is choice silver because it brings forth the precious treasures in the heart of the righteous, but the heart of the wicked is empty, and his words have no value, revealing the work of the wicked one in the soul.

10.20.3.en: * The commandments of the Lord are pure commandments, refined by fire, tried on the earth, purified seven times (Ps 12:6).

10.20.4.en: As silver is refined, so the righteous man is tested, and becomes God's coin and receives the royal image. Or as the wise Solomon says: "The tongue of the righteous is like gold refined by fire," hinting that firmly established and wise teaching is accepted and praised, and it is sufficiently refined on earth, meaning that the soul of the Gnostic (the possessor of spiritual knowledge) is made holy in many ways when it is withdrawn from the earthly fire.

10.20.5.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Origen sees that gold points to understanding and thought, while silver points to language and the power of speech. Therefore the cherubim are described as being of gold, because they are full of knowledge, and the golden lampstand that was placed in the tabernacle of meeting also points to the natural law that holds the light of knowledge.

10.21.0.en: The lips of the righteous feed (guide) many: but fools die for want of understanding (wisdom) [21]

10.21.1.en: The speech of the righteous carries no folly, and no bad word comes out of his mouth, but he offers all that is for the building up of his own soul and the building up of his brothers. He regards his mouth as a consecrated instrument bearing the words of the Lord, which are uttered in a spirit fitting to an ambassador of Christ. Goodness, or the righteousness of Christ declared by the lips of the righteous, feeds the soul with angelic bread as it feeds other souls, and so drives all toward growth; but folly, ignorance, or evil cannot keep its owner alive, for it destroys him with hunger.

10.21.2.en: Since the Lord Christ, the divine Wisdom, speaks through the lips of the righteous, He offers Himself to the hearers as spiritual food that satisfies souls, while fools speak much to offer, out of the emptiness of their hearts and thoughts, death to their own souls and the souls of their hearers.

10.21.3.en: Here we see in Samuel the judge and prophet, and Saul the king, a witness to what is said in this proverb, for Samuel's aim was to offer blessing to the thousands of the people, but Saul gained nothing from being chosen king, nor did he benefit from the presence of the great Samuel among the prophets.

10.22.0.en: "The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no toil with it" [22]

10.22.1.en: The blessing of the Lord alone is able truly to enrich life, but does it really add no toil with it?! How does this agree with what Holy Scripture and practical reality bear witness to, that the tribulations of the righteous are many? The true believer touches the blessing of the Lord in his joys and sorrows, in all the circumstances of his life, so he feels the richness of God's transcendent providence, and perceives God's mysteries and His plan toward him, and does not feel the toil.

10.23.0.en: "To do wickedness is as sport to a fool: but wisdom is for a man of understanding" [23]

10.23.1.en: Since the fool does not carry the fear of the Lord in his heart, he cares for nothing, but the wise man has his heart, his thought, his words, and his conduct ruled by the fear of the Lord, and he walks in the spirit of the Holy God.

10.23.2.en: The Book of Numbers presents to us the character of Phinehas the priest, who was zealous for the holiness of the people of God and the sanctity of the divine holy things, and took a firm stand, by which God turned away His wrath from His people (Num 25:6-13). On the contrary, Balaam was foolish, despite God's declarations to him not to curse the people of God, but love of the gift made him waver, and it reached the point that he was rebuked by the donkey he was riding (Num 22:28).

10.23.3.en: The fool, or the foolish man, is the one who practices vice and delights in it, counting the harm to his own inner depths and the harm to his brothers as laughter and amusement. He does not care about his eternity as though it were an illusion, and does not care for the comfort and peace of his brothers.

10.23.4.en: Jesters turn their lives into a kind of amusement, so they utter jests, thinking that they are creating an atmosphere of fun, sometimes using false words, and perhaps wounding some of the hearers under the cover of humor.

10.23.5.en: But the wise man finds his amusement and delight in his fellowship with God and his enjoyment of new daily experiences on the royal way under the guidance of the Holy Spirit of God who dwells in him.

10.23.6.en: Let the believer realize that his mouth is God's embassy, speaking the message of salvation, bearing witness to the new life in Christ Jesus, and proclaiming the heavenly life.

10.23.7.en: * They said to him (St. Abba Anthony): What is the meaning of the Apostle's saying: "Rejoice in the Lord"? He said: [If we rejoice in doing the commandments, this is rejoicing in the Lord; let us rejoice in fulfilling the commandments of the Lord and in the success of our brothers, and let us keep ourselves from the joy of the world and from laughter if we want to be among the special ones of our Lord, for He said that the world will rejoice, and you will weep (Jn 16:20), and He said that woe to those who laugh and blessed are those who weep (Lk 6:21, 25). And it is not written that He ever laughed, but it is written that He was grieved and His eyes shed tears (Jn 11:35).]

10.23.8.en: St. Abba Anthony the Great * Familiarity, jesting, and laughter are like a fire kindled in reeds, and they destroy.

10.23.9.en: Abba Agathon * Take care not to open your mouth in laughter, for laughter shows a lack of the fear of God.

10.23.10.en: St. Abba Isaiah * Because we do not guard against small slips, we fall into great ones. For example, a person's laughing at the wrong time draws another to laugh, and then he says: What harm is there in laughter? Then the fear of God begins to be uprooted from him, and from laughter jesting is born, and from jesting ugly speech, and from these come blameworthy deeds. So the deceiving enemy makes small slips easy for us and from them draws us into great sins.

10.24.0.en: 24 The fear of the wicked, it shall come upon him: but the desire of the righteous shall be granted. 25 As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation. 26 As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him. 27 The fear of the LORD prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened. 28 The expectation of the righteous shall be gladness: but the hope of the wicked shall perish.

10.24.1.en: "The fear of the wicked, it shall come upon him: but the desire of the righteous shall be granted" [24]

10.24.2.en: The wicked often appear as jesters who create an atmosphere of fun and joy, and boast of their ability to do so, but their depths are filled with fear and disturbance, and peace finds no place in their depths. In their depths they think that by their jesting they lighten their terrible inner feelings and the burdens of others, but soon their inner fears are realized. As for the righteous, the desire of their heart is the glory of God, the salvation of the world, and the building up of their souls; all these are divine gifts that God offers them freely. It is as though God gives every person the hidden desire of his heart. The fearful wicked man falls into fear, and the righteous man who cares for eternity enjoys it. It is as though in the end a person faces the sum of his inner depths: either he receives unutterable glory, or falls into a shame that cannot be removed.

10.24.3.en: "As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more:

10.25.0.en: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation" [25]

10.25.1.en: Some regard this verse, together with the preceding verse, as one complete proverb. The wicked man, who bears the image of courage, strength, authority, and happiness, is ruled by fear, anxiety, and gloom, and passes like a whirlwind that no sooner blows than it disappears and becomes as though it had never been. But the righteous man, in the midst of his trials and tribulations, has his inner being filled with great joy, for the Lord grants him the desire of his heart, and makes him like a temple founded on foundations that support him eternally.

10.25.2.en: The wicked man casts himself under the divine wrath, and the fruits of his evil pass over him like a tornado (a cyclone) that shakes the whole city, sweeps away its buildings, and topples its trees, leaving neither branch nor root but uprooting trees with their roots. But the righteous man, whose soul is founded on eternity, cannot be shaken by all the whirlwinds of the world, for the hairs of his head are numbered by his heavenly Father, and he is hidden in the Rock of Ages and is not moved. The practical example in the Old Testament is the prophet Daniel and those who accused him. Daniel was thrown into the lions' den and spent the most wonderful night he had lived in all the days of his life, while his accusers thought they had succeeded in carrying out their plan, but soon the lions devoured them.

10.25.3.en: * When the storm blows, the wicked perish, but the righteous, since they avoid it, are saved forever. When temptation attacks, the wicked easily fall into sin. On the other hand, the righteous are saved eternally when they overcome temptation with patience and a soul thankful to God. See how righteousness carries security, for the righteous are saved when they avoid evil, for they take a defensive position and stand firm at all times. On the other hand the wicked fall even when no temptation attacks them at all. Therefore those who are ignorant of God's just judgment sin easily.

10.26.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him" [26]

10.26.1.en: As vinegar spoils the teeth and smoke the eyes, so whoever relies on a sluggard finds that he does not return to those who sent him with the required results, but causes them a state of frustration and great anxiety. As the Lord Christ offers Himself as heavenly bread that the believer eats and lives and is satisfied, sin offers itself as food or vinegar that spoils the teeth.

10.26.2.en: The Lord Christ gave us the parable of the slothful servant (Lk 19:20-26), who did not trade with the talent given to him, nor even give it to the bankers so that he might benefit from the profit (interest), but buried it in the earth, justifying this by insulting his master, saying: "For I feared thee, because thou art an austere man: thou takest up that thou layedst not down, and reapest that thou didst not sow" (Lk 19:21).

10.27.0.en: "The fear of the LORD prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened" [27]

10.27.1.en: Perhaps you will say that many who feared the Lord died as children or young people, like the martyrs Abanoub and the sons of St. Rebecca and Mother Dolagi... Although they died as children, their life in the eyes of the Lord is far longer than that of wicked old men without spiritual fruit. The measure of a person's age in God's eyes is not counted by the time we live but by the work we offer.

10.27.2.en: The fear of the Lord lengthens a person's days, for the grace of God is added to him, so that a day becomes for him as a thousand years. But the wicked man, deprived of the fear of the Lord, loses his eternity and falls under the judgment of bitter Gehenna.

10.28.0.en: "The expectation of the LORD is gladness: but the hope of the wicked shall perish" [28]

10.28.1.en: Besides the blessing that the one who fears the Lord receives, so that every moment of his life is valued as long, fruitful years, the fear of the Lord fills his life with hope of meeting with God and enjoying the fellowship of the glories, so he lives rejoicing in the Spirit and pours out this joy on others.

10.28.2.en: The righteous man awaits his eternity and the eternity of his brothers with joy in the midst of the pains of this world, but the wicked man's hope is in temporal things which, even if he obtains them, soon pass away. The wicked man who persists in not repenting, even if he hopes for God's mercies, loses this vain hope through his persistence in not repenting and his continual negligence.

10.28.3.en: It is said of Alexander the Great that he was never satisfied; he wept because he found no other worlds to open and subject to his kingdom, and he died at about 33 years of age, and died almost like a suicide.

10.28.4.en: And Hannibal, who filled three huge bushels with gold rings taken from those he slaughtered, ended his life by suicide with poison.

10.28.5.en: Julius Caesar, whose garments were dyed with the blood of a million of his enemies, who defeated 800 cities, was wounded by his dearest friend at the scene of his great triumph.

10.28.6.en: Napoleon, the feared conqueror, who had been the punisher, spent his last days punished.

10.29.0.en: 29 The way of the LORD is strength to the upright: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity. 30 The righteous shall never be removed: but the wicked shall not inhabit the earth.

10.29.1.en: "The way of the LORD is a fortress to the upright: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity" [29]

10.29.2.en: The believer finds strength in the way of the Lord, seeing in God a fortress and a tower that protects him, and in obedience to Him a renewal of his vitality, and as he works striving, he sings, saying: "The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation."

10.29.4.en: "The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God is my rock, in whom I take refuge; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my refuge" (Ps 18:2).

10.29.5.en: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" (Ps 27:1).

10.29.6.en: "The LORD is their strength, and he is the saving strength of his anointed" (Ps 28:8).

10.29.7.en: "Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily: be thou my strong rock, a fortress, an house of defence to save me" (Ps 31:2).

10.29.8.en: "Pull me out of the net that they have laid privily for me: for thou art my fortress" (Ps 31:4).

10.30.0.en: "The righteous shall never be removed: but the wicked shall not inhabit the earth" [30]

10.30.1.en: The wicked rejoice, thinking that the earth is their eternal dwelling, but in a moment they leave it, as though they had passed over it like a shadow and had not dwelt in it. Even if they live in palaces they are counted as those in exile or as wanderers without shelter, because their depths do not enjoy stability. But the righteous man sets up his dwelling on an eternal foundation, which death cannot remove; he feels security and stability, even if he is imprisoned.

10.30.2.en: Holy Scripture presents us with practical examples such as Cain and Abel, for Abel died, but though he died his blood cries out (Gen 4:10)! But Cain lived on the earth as a fugitive, pursued by fear wherever he settled. So also Isaac and Ishmael, the latter wanted to kill Isaac while jesting with him! So also Jacob and Esau.

10.31.0.en: 31 The mouth of the just bringeth forth wisdom: but the froward tongue shall be cut out. 32 The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable: but the mouth of the wicked speaketh frowardness.

10.31.1.en: The chapter closes with two statements about the tongue [31-32]. Having already presented examples of the wise mouth and the holy tongue, he returns to affirm the importance of sanctifying the mouth and the tongue.

10.31.2.en: "The mouth of the just bringeth forth wisdom: but the froward tongue shall be cut out" [31]

10.31.3.en: The mouth of the righteous is like a tree that bears wisdom, growing without ceasing, satisfying the hearts of many, but the tongue that utters lies, a time comes when it is cut off from the world without benefit.

10.31.4.en: Perhaps by the tongue of lies he means opposition to the true faith, and uttering blasphemy against God or deviation from the true faith.

10.32.0.en: "The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable: but the mouth of the wicked speaketh frowardness" [32]

10.32.1.en: The righteous utter what pleases God and gives Him joy, so they offer the truth for the building up of many souls, but the wicked utter destructive blasphemies.

10.32.2.en: * Do not keep company with the one of harsh tongue or the proud of heart.

10.32.3.en: St. Abba Paul of Tamoh * If we keep the right faith and keep the body from fornication and the tongue from slander, then by the grace of God we are prospering according to this age.

10.32.5.en: Grant me Your heavenly wisdom, and my life will be exalted by Your grace!

10.32.6.en: * Grant me Your wisdom, O holy Father, that I may walk as Your son, ascend to the heights of loftiness, and You will rejoice in me, O Father wonderful in His love!

10.32.7.en: * Grant me not to allow my follies to rule over me, nor my foolishness to make me lose my attachment to You, lest Jerusalem above, my mother, grieve because of me!

10.32.8.en: * Let me possess the righteousness of Christ, and my soul will overflow with satisfaction.

10.32.9.en: And my heart will be filled with the treasures of Your knowledge.

10.32.10.en: I do not desire the riches of the world and its treasures.

10.32.11.en: You are my wealth and the treasures of my soul!

10.32.12.en: * I will walk by Your Spirit who never ceases to work.

10.32.13.en: In the spirit of diligence and sincerity I will work with You.

10.32.14.en: Then my soul will be enriched by You, O Supreme Good.

10.32.15.en: I will not suffer want or poverty or hunger!

10.32.16.en: I do not know idleness, nor do I seek the rest of the world, but I rejoice in striving by Your grace, and I find my rest in You alone!

10.32.17.en: * You give me the spirit of uprightness and simplicity.

10.32.18.en: I will not turn to the right or to the left.

10.32.19.en: Then Your blessings will come upon my head.

10.32.20.en: And deceit and craftiness will find no place in my thought or heart!

10.32.21.en: * By Your grace I bear Your blessings.

10.32.22.en: You support me in my sojourn, and keep my memory after my departure!

10.32.23.en: Here I bow before Your commandment in a spirit of obedience; I rejoice in it as a treasure I hide in my heart.

10.32.24.en: My soul exults in it, and my whole being is filled with heavenly peace!

10.32.25.en: * By Your commandment I walk uprightly, and all my senses and emotions are in harmony with my words and my conduct.

10.32.26.en: My whole being becomes a spiritual harp, upon which Your Holy Spirit plays the symphony of eternal love!

10.32.27.en: * A fountain will arise in me overflowing with living waters.

10.32.28.en: And my tongue will be sanctified, speaking only according to Your grace!

10.32.29.en: My life will become a love that never ceases; I cover the faults of my brothers, and You cover my sins with the blood of the Crucified!

10.32.30.en: * My mouth overflows with Your wisdom, and my soul exults as the light of Your knowledge shines upon me!

10.32.31.en: * My life becomes a delightful journey; with every morning my soul sets out as to heaven!

10.32.32.en: My insight is dazzled by the splendor of Your glory.

10.32.33.en: And my tongue is silent in amazement before the throne of Your grace!

10.32.34.en: I long for silence that I may hear Your voice, O Beloved.

10.32.35.en: And I long for You to speak through me, that my brothers may enjoy Your mysteries with me.

10.32.36.en: * I know neither jesting nor laughter, and my soul knows neither gloom nor bitterness.

10.32.37.en: I cherish every second of my life, because You never cease to work in me in Your bounty.

10.32.38.en: * My soul is filled with Your fear, O Lover of mankind.

10.32.39.en: Then I grow continually by receiving the abundance of Your wisdom.

10.32.40.en: I live in security, for I take refuge in Your embrace.

10.32.41.en: For You are the secret of my joy, my satisfaction, and my eternal peace.
